newsitem.title: USA: CNET slumps after first quarter earnings.
newsitem.headline: CNET slumps after first quarter earnings.

text.p: Shares of The Computer Network Inc lost over 20 percent of its value on Friday following a first quarter earnings statement that disappointed some and puzzled others.

CNET fell 4-5/8 to 18-1/4 in light afternoon trading on Nasdaq. On Thursday CNET posted a first-quarter loss of $12.9 million, or $0.97 a share, on revenues of $6.3 million. Without charges the loss per share would have been $0.28, better than the $0.30 a share analysts had expected, according to First Call.
In the year-ago quarter the company lost $3.7 million, or $0.40 a share on revenues of $1.65 million.
Based in San Francisco, CNET is a media company specializing in Internet sites tailored for the technology-savvy user. It also makes computer-related television programs.

Daniel Rimer, an analyst at Hambrecht & Quist said the reason behind the stock's fall on Friday was caused by general volitility in the technology stock sector coupled with weak advertising revenue growth as well as a charge that CNET took against earnings.
"Investors are wondering and speculating what CNET is putting $2.2 million of investment into," Rimer said.

CNET's charge against first quarter earnings included $2.2 million for a new, unannounced online venture. The company declined to give details about the venture but said it will make an announcement in the second quarter. CNET is said to have 70 staff working on the venture for the past nine months.

"The Internet environment is a lot more competitive than the majority of environments out there and they have chosen for competitive reasons to disclose the nature of the venture at a later date," Rimer said.

Traffic on CNET's nine Internet sites, which include the popular http://www.news.com, increased 42 percent to 3.24 million average daily page views from 2.28 million average daily page views in the previous quarter.

Despite the big increase in page views, or hits, advertising revenues rose only three percent to $4.54 million from $4.41 million in the fourth quarter putting a question mark on expectations of explosive growth in advertising dollars.

The small growth was attributed to traditional seasonal reductions in ad spending among computer and technology advertisers, which account for about 90 percent of CNET's ad base. Advertisers on CNET's Internet sites grew to 111 in the first quarter from 101 in the previous quarter.

Rimer, who rates the stock a buy, noted that CNET managed to increase traffic by 42 percent while decreasing the amount spent on marketing by 28 percent when compared with the previous quarter. In the fourth quarter it grew traffic by 50 percent while cutting marketing costs by 60 percent, he said.

"The reason for that is that they can cross-promote across their network of Internet sites ... the more they develop their business model the cheaper it becomes for them to grow their business model," Rimer said.
"From a fundamental perspective the story remains extremely strong," he said.
